meta.title: HotkeyDetective — Find out which app stole your keyboard shortcut
meta.desc: A free menu-bar utility for macOS that identifies which app owns a keyboard shortcut. It gathers evidence from five independent sources and shows you the reasoning, so you can judge the answer instead of trusting it. Notarized, open source, 15 languages.
og.desc: macOS gives you no way to ask which app owns a shortcut. This does — and it shows its evidence.
hero.lede:
You press <kbd>⇧⌘4</kbd> and nothing happens. Some app took it — but which one?
      macOS ships no API that answers this, and no way to ask in System Settings either.
hero.shotAlt: HotkeyDetective showing that Maccy, Ice and Spotlight have all registered ⌘Space, with four pieces of evidence listed beneath
hero.caption: Press the combination. Get an answer — and the reasoning behind it.
how.title: It gathers evidence, then weighs it
how.sub:
There is no single source of truth for “who owns this shortcut,” so the app collects
      independent signals and tells you which one it is leaning on.
src.system.p:
Reads macOS’s own shortcut table — the authoritative one behind System Settings — and the
           overrides you have made to it.
src.config.p:
Parses the settings files of apps it knows, so it can name the exact action —
           not just the app.
src.config.s: High — lower when the app isn’t running
src.scan.p:
Recognizes two common shortcut-storage formats in any app’s settings, so unfamiliar
           apps are not automatically invisible.
src.reaction.p:
Watches what actually happens after the keypress — an app opening a window or coming
           to the front within milliseconds.
src.probe.p:
Asks the Carbon hotkey API whether the combination is already spoken for. Honest about
           its ceiling — see the limits below.
src.verdict.p:
Every claim shows the evidence it rests on, so you can judge the answer yourself rather
           than trusting a black box.
ladder.title: Five answers, not one
ladder.sub: A shortcut is rarely a clean yes or no. The verdict says how sure it is.
ladder.confirmed.p:
An authoritative source binds this combination. The system table said so, or a known app’s
           settings did while the app is running.
ladder.likely.p:
The evidence points one way but does not settle it — a scan match, or an app that reacted
           without a registration to back it up.
ladder.contested.p:
Two or more owners registered the same combination. This is the case you came here for,
           and it is pinned to the top of the inventory.
ladder.occupied.p:
Something holds it, but nothing identified who. Rare in practice — the limits section
           explains why.
ladder.free.p: Nothing found. Safe to assign — with the same caveat as above.
callout.h: The distinction that makes it trustworthy
callout.p1: A reaction proves an app received the key. It does not prove the app registered it. So a reaction can corroborate an owner — but it can never contest one.
callout.p2:
Without that rule, <kbd>⌘Space</kbd> reads as “the system and Spotlight are fighting” when
        nothing is wrong at all: Spotlight is simply what the system shortcut opens. Getting this
        backwards is what makes a conflict detector cry wolf, and it is the reason every verdict here
        shows its sources instead of a single confident sentence.
inv.title: Or skip the guessing entirely
inv.sub:
Beyond one-shot probing, the app lists every shortcut it can see — system bindings, known apps
      and scan results — with conflicts pinned to the top.
inv.shotAlt: The inventory window listing every known shortcut with its owner and evidence source
inv.caption: Search by combination or app. Deep scan additionally reads sandboxed apps’ settings — macOS asks permission per app, so it is off by default.
priv.title: What it does with your keystrokes
priv.sub: Short version: watches one, keeps one, sends none.
priv.1: There is no network code in the repository. Nothing is uploaded, because nothing can be.
priv.2: The keyboard tap is listen-only. Keys are observed, never intercepted — the real owner still receives them. That is exactly how reaction detection works.
priv.3: Nothing is logged or stored. The only key data that survives a probe is the single combination you chose to look up.
priv.4: Permissions are explained, not demanded. The probe needs Accessibility and Input Monitoring, because macOS requires both for a listen-only tap.
priv.5: It still works without them. In limited mode you pick a combination manually and it answers from settings files alone.
priv.6: The source is public. MIT licensed — every claim on this page is checkable.
lim.title: What it cannot do
lim.sub: A detector that hides its blind spots is worse than no detector.
lim.1.h: Carbon hotkey probing cannot see other processes
lim.1.p: RegisterEventHotKey reports a conflict only within the calling process, which makes the “occupied but unidentified” verdict effectively unreachable. An app that registers a hotkey, shows no window, and stores its config in an unrecognized format stays invisible.
lim.2.h: System feature names are English outside Korean
lim.2.p:
macOS keeps its own translations somewhere we cannot read. Inventing replacements would
           disagree with what you see in System Settings, so the original English name is shown instead.
lim.3.h: Config scanning recognizes two storage formats
lim.3.p: The KeyboardShortcuts library and MASShortcut-style dictionaries. Apps with custom formats need a dedicated parser —
ins.title: Install
ins.sub: Requires macOS 14 or later. Free, and there is nothing to unlock.
ins.brew.p: There is no in-app updater, so this is the path that keeps you current — brew upgrade does the rest.
ins.dmg.p: A notarized disk image, about a megabyte. Open it and drag the app to Applications.
ins.src.p: Signs with your own Developer ID if the keychain has one, ad-hoc otherwise.
langs.title: Speaks your language
langs.sub: The interface follows your system language. No setting to find.
foot.made: Built by the team behind Unifyl, a dual-pane file manager for macOS.
